paras: The Steve Green extradition case was a 1910 effort by Black Chicagoans to keep Steve Green, a Black farm worker charged with killing a white planter near Jericho, Arkansas, from being returned to Arkansas to be lynched. An Arkansas officer taking Green south was stopped at Cairo, Illinois, by a telegraphed habeas corpus writ, and on September 19 a Chicago judge discharged him. The Black press hailed the outcome as a rescue from lynching.

In Green's account, printed by the Broad Ax, he had worked under contract for the planter for 'a bare pittance' and announced he would leave for a farmer offering more. The planter's name appeared as Sedlas, Sidel, Sadler, Sidle and Seidle, and the killing was dated 'last February', March 18 or 'last spring'.

Green said the planter came to his cabin with three friends on horseback and shot him four times, after which he got his gun and fired once. The Cairo Bulletin instead reported that shots hit him as he escaped 'from the crowd at Jericho after the murder.' Green said he then evaded bloodhounds by filling his shoes with pepper and rolling among hogs.

Arrested in Chicago in August, reportedly after George Chivers turned him in, Green said he would be burned if returned and asked to be allowed to kill himself. On August 23 the police handed him to an Arkansas officer, named as Sheriff C. L. Lewis in wire reports and as deputy Ed Munroe by the Cairo Bulletin, despite a pending habeas petition. On a telegram from the Cook County sheriff, Sheriff Fred D. Nellis took Green off the train at Cairo and returned him to Chicago. Green later said his custodian had told him 'a reception committee of a thousand' waited 'with a lighted fire', and the Defender reported talk of a mob of 2,000.

Rev. A. J. Carey and Edward D. Green asked Governor Charles S. Deneen not to grant extradition, and a mass meeting at the Institutional Church formed a permanent committee. Sheriff Lewis replied that Crittenden County people had no thought of lynching Green. A municipal judge refused to hold Chicago police officials in contempt for surrendering Green.

On September 19 Judge Richard S. Tuthill ruled that the police had no right to surrender Green and discharged him after attorneys Edward H. Wright and William G. Anderson argued the case. One dispatch said the ground was that Green was not named in the indictment, and that Black spectators applauded until reprimanded. Arkansas could still seek his return if he left Illinois.

White coverage came mainly through brief Associated Press dispatches in Alabama, Texas and Kentucky papers that called Green 'a negro' charged with murder and left the fear of lynching to his defenders' words. The Cairo Bulletin headlined 'NEGRO IS RESCUED' and 'Mob Was Ready' yet called Green a 'Wretch' and the lynching fear 'the excuse' for stopping him. The Cotter Courier printed his pleas in mocking dialect, while a Wisconsin weekly said the discharge checked 'possible lynching and race rioting.'

The Chicago Defender headlined 'CHICAGO POLICE GIVES COLORED MAN UP TO LYNCHERS' and blamed 'a dirty set of Irish policemen' and Chivers. After the discharge the Broad Ax and the Defender ran one long account praising Wright and Anderson, crediting Ida B. Wells-Barnett, and likening the rescue to 'the many miraculous escapes of our fore fathers in slavery days.'
Every version of the shooting came from Green or the Chicago police: Green claimed self-defense, police said he confessed, and one dispatch said the men exchanged shots.

reader.title: Steve Green extradition case
bases: Green, a Black man accused of killing a white planter, was wounded by shots as he fled (A4, A27) and was threatened with mob burning if returned to Arkansas (A20, A28); his removal was stopped for fear of lynching (A4, A6) and no mob killing occurred.

No one was killed by a mob: Green was wounded and escaped (A4, A27), was threatened with a mob of 2,000 or 'a thousand' (A20, A28), and was discharged in Chicago (A22, A24); the only death reported is the planter Green was accused of killing (A3, A5).

The local Cairo Bulletin (A4), Associated Press dispatches (A5, A6), the Chicago Defender (A13, A14) and the Broad Ax (A24, A26) independently report Green's arrest, the interception at Cairo for fear of lynching, and his discharge; the shooting at Jericho itself is known only from Green's statements and one Cairo line (A4, A27).

accounts.label: Chicago police / AP 'confession'
accounts.gist: Green confessed to Inspector Wheeler that he shot and killed the planter during an argument over working a farm on shares.

accounts.label: Cairo Bulletin (local, after questioning Green)
accounts.gist: Several shots were fired at Green as he escaped the crowd at Jericho after the killing, and Arkansas people were 'bent on lynching him'.

accounts.label: Arkansas sheriff
accounts.gist: Sheriff Lewis said the people of Crittenden County had no notion of lynching Green and that he would protect him, with militia if needed.

accounts.label: Chicago Black leaders
accounts.gist: Green could not get a fair trial in Arkansas and would be mobbed and burned; Arkansas officers had told him a mob would meet him.

framing.detail: Short AP dispatches ('SHERIFF STOPPED BY COURT PAPER', 'FEAR FOR NEGRO'S LIFE') called Green 'a negro' charged with murder and attributed the lynching fear to his Chicago defenders.
The Cairo Bulletin headlined 'NEGRO IS RESCUED' and 'Mob Was Ready' but called Green a 'Wretch' and 'the negro murdererer' and the lynching fear 'the excuse' for his return.
The Cotter Courier printed Green's pleas in mocking dialect; a Wisconsin paper said the discharge checked 'possible lynching and race rioting'.
The Defender headlined 'CHICAGO POLICE GIVES COLORED MAN UP TO LYNCHERS', attacked the Harrison Street police and Chivers, and called Arkansas 'Hell'.
The Broad Ax and Defender hailed the discharge as a legal precedent won by Black attorneys and likened Green's escape to slavery-era flights from 'lynching'.
